notes:
Task and constraints: Count the bit positions where integers x and y differ.
Idea: XOR x and y, then repeatedly clear the lowest set bit while counting iterations.
Technique and why it applies: XOR sets a bit precisely where the inputs differ. The operation z &= z-1 removes one set bit from z, so the loop count equals the Hamming distance.
Invariant: distance equals the number of set bits already removed from z.
Edge cases: Equal values produce z=0 and return zero. Under the usual fixed-width integer model, at most a fixed number of bits are examined.
Complexity: The loop is O(w) for w-bit integers and O(1) auxiliary space. The author O(1) time label assumes fixed-width machine integers.

Task and constraints: Minimize the sum of absolute differences between array values and one chosen target value.
Idea: Sort the array and choose its median, then sum distances to that value.
Technique and why it applies: The median minimizes the sum of absolute deviations. For even length, this code chooses the floor of the average of the two middle values, which is also between them and therefore also minimizes the sum for integer targets.
Invariant: After sorting, the selected median is a minimizing target for absolute-distance cost.
Edge cases: The code assumes nums is nonempty. Sorting mutates the input list; for even length, integer division chooses the lower central value when their sum is odd.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n), and summing distances takes O(n), for O(n log n) time and O(1) explicit auxiliary space apart from sorting temporaries.

Task and constraints: Compute the perimeter of the land region in a grid of land and water cells.
Idea: Add four edges for each land cell, then subtract two for every shared edge with the land cell above or to the left.
Technique and why it applies: Every land cell initially contributes four exposed edges. Each shared land-land edge was counted twice, so subtracting two removes its internal contribution exactly once.
Invariant: perimeter equals the count of cell edges not shared with another land cell processed earlier or adjacent above/left.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty rectangular grid. It relies on checking only top and left neighbors so each shared edge is handled once.
Complexity: Every cell is scanned once, giving O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the total perimeter of land cells in a rectangular binary grid.
Idea: Count land cells and count adjacent land pairs, then compute four times the cell count minus twice the shared-edge count.
Technique and why it applies: Each land cell contributes four sides; each adjacent pair shares one internal edge that must be removed from both cells' perimeter totals. Only top and left neighbors are counted to avoid double counting.
Invariant: count is the number of land cells and repeat is the number of shared edges seen so far.
Edge cases: Empty grid handling is not explicit; the problem normally guarantees at least one row and column. The imported operator module is unused.
Complexity: A single scan gives O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the first player can force a win in the number-picking game without reusing a chosen integer.
Idea: Recursively try each remaining number and memoize game states keyed by the accumulated total and remaining-number tuple.
Technique and why it applies: A move wins immediately if it reaches the desired total; otherwise a player can force a win when any move leaves the opponent unable to win. The code treats a state already at or above the target as a loss for the player to move.
Invariant: can_win(total,remainder) represents whether the current player can force a win from that state.
Edge cases: desiredTotal==0 returns True, and if the sum of all choices is too small the method returns False. The snippet uses @cache without importing it, so it fails unless that decorator is defined externally.
Complexity: Memoization can still visit exponentially many subsets, up to O(2^M) states for M=maxChoosableInteger, with O(M) state-key and recursion storage per active path.

Task and constraints: Count how many times s2 repeated n2 times can fit as a subsequence in s1 repeated n1 times.
Idea: Precompute, for every position in s2, the ending position and completed-match count after scanning one copy of s1.
Technique and why it applies: dp[i] records the next s2 position and how many full s2 copies were completed while consuming one s1 block. Repeating the transition n1 times accumulates matches, then division by n2 converts to the requested repetition count.
Invariant: next is the current matched-prefix position in s2, and res counts full s2 matches across processed s1 copies.
Edge cases: n2 must be positive. Empty s2 is outside usual constraints because len(s2) controls the DP state list and division by n2 is performed.
Complexity: Precomputation is O(|s1||s2|), and simulation is O(n1), with O(|s2|) auxiliary storage. For large n1, this repeated transition loop can be too slow.

Task and constraints: Count distinct nonempty substrings of p that occur in the infinite alphabet wraparound string.
Idea: Split p into maximal consecutive wraparound runs and record the longest run starting at each character.
Technique and why it applies: Every prefix of a valid run starting at a given character is also a valid wraparound substring. Keeping the maximum length per starting letter counts each such substring once by its start and length.
Invariant: map_[c] is the greatest valid wraparound substring length starting with character c found so far.
Edge cases: get_next wraps z to a. The snippet uses collections.defaultdict without importing collections, so that name must be supplied externally or execution fails.
Complexity: The outer loop advances through maximal runs, and the inner loop visits each character in its run once; across all runs this totals O(n) work. The fixed alphabet map uses O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Count distinct substrings of p that appear in the infinite wraparound alphabet string.
Idea: Track the current consecutive wraparound run length and the longest such run ending at each letter.
Technique and why it applies: A run ending in a character contributes all lengths up to its current length, but only lengths beyond the previous maximum for that ending character are new. The fixed 26-element array stores these maxima.
Invariant: letters[c] is the maximum valid run length ending at letter c, and result sums newly counted lengths.
Edge cases: The wraparound condition handles z followed by a. If a character breaks the sequence, length resets before counting the new one-character run.
Complexity: One pass with fixed-size array updates gives O(n) time and O(1) space, matching the author labels.

Task and constraints: Classify a string as a valid IPv4 address, valid IPv6 address, or Neither under the specified block rules.
Idea: Replace dots with colons, count nonempty blocks, then validate four decimal-like blocks or eight hexadecimal-like blocks.
Technique and why it applies: Block count chooses the candidate address family. The code then checks emptiness, numeric characters, leading zeros and bounds for IPv4, or character membership and maximum length for IPv6.
Invariant: A candidate is returned as valid only after each block passes the checks in its selected branch.
Edge cases: The IPv4 range and leading-zero checks are inside the len(i)>1 condition, so a one-character numeric field is not range-checked; for example, 999.1.1.1 can be incorrectly accepted. isnumeric can also accept Unicode numeric characters outside ASCII digits.
Complexity: Splitting and scanning the string a constant number of times gives O(n) time and O(n) space for the replaced string and split lists.

Task and constraints: Return IPv4, IPv6, or Neither according to the address's exact syntax.
Idea: Split on dots and validate four decimal octets; if that fails structurally, split on colons and validate eight hexadecimal groups.
Technique and why it applies: IPv4 blocks must be decimal values from 0 to 255 without leading zeros. IPv6 blocks must contain one to four hexadecimal digits. string.hexdigits supplies the accepted hex alphabet.
Invariant: The address is accepted only if every block meets its family-specific syntax and block-count requirements.
Edge cases: Empty blocks are rejected by the length checks. The IPv4 branch indexes blocks[i][0], but short-circuiting ensures a nonempty block was already established by isdigit only if that check succeeds.
Complexity: Each address character is examined a constant number of times, so O(n) time and O(n) space for split blocks.

Task and constraints: Return words that can be formed by concatenating at least two shorter words from the provided dictionary.
Idea: Recursively split each word into dictionary prefixes and check whether the suffix can also be decomposed.
Technique and why it applies: set_words supports constant-time expected membership tests. The first recursive call excludes taking the entire word as one component; once a component has been chosen, the remaining suffix may be accepted as a dictionary word.
Invariant: check(word,seen) tests whether the suffix can be segmented after the already chosen pieces represented by seen.
Edge cases: Empty suffix returns True. The seen set is passed but never used to prevent reuse, so it is redundant; recursion may repeatedly explore the same suffix states without memoization.
Complexity: Prefix exploration can be exponential in word length in the worst case, with recursive slicing and set creation adding overhead. Space is proportional to recursion depth and temporary substrings.

Task and constraints: Identify dictionary words that consist of at least two other words from the list concatenated together.
Idea: For each word, use a boolean DP array to mark prefixes that can be formed from dictionary words shorter than the whole word.
Technique and why it applies: dp[i] means the prefix of length i is segmentable. From each reachable i, the code checks every later endpoint j and marks dp[j] when word[i:j] is in lookup, excluding the full word itself.
Invariant: dp[j] is True exactly when a valid decomposition of the prefix ending at j has been found.
Edge cases: The strict j-i < len(word) condition prevents a word from validating itself as a single component. The code assumes words contain no duplicates as stated.
Complexity: For each of W words of maximum length L, DP checks O(L²) substrings, giving O(WL²) time and O(L) temporary DP space plus O(total dictionary characters) storage. Author labels are rough if n means word count.

Task and constraints: Determine whether every matchstick can be used exactly once to form four equal-length square sides.
Idea: Reject totals not divisible by four, sort sticks largest first, then backtrack assigning each stick to one of four side sums.
Technique and why it applies: Descending order exposes oversized sticks early. A placement is skipped if it exceeds target; after failure, the stick is removed from that side. The empty-side break avoids symmetric equivalent branches.
Invariant: targetLst stores the partial sum assigned to each side for the sticks already processed.
Edge cases: The code assumes matchsticks is nonempty because it reads matchsticks[0]. Sorting mutates the input. The final equal-sums test is reached only after all sticks are assigned.
Complexity: Backtracking is exponential in the number of sticks in the worst case, though sorting and symmetry pruning reduce search. Auxiliary space is O(n) for recursion plus O(1) side sums.

Task and constraints: Maximize the number of binary strings selected while using at most m zeros and n ones.
Idea: Use a two-dimensional 0/1 knapsack DP indexed by available one-count and zero-count budgets.
Technique and why it applies: For each string, count zeros and ones, then update capacities downward so the current string cannot be selected multiple times in the same iteration. dp[i][j] stores the largest subset size within those budgets.
Invariant: After processing each string, every DP state represents the best subset using only strings processed so far.
Edge cases: An empty string would cost no zeros or ones and be selected once per item iteration; usual constraints provide nonempty binary strings. The dimensions are indexed as [ones][zeros].
Complexity: For each of W strings, the nested capacity loops cost O(mn), yielding O(Wmn) time and O(mn) space.

Task and constraints: Find the largest subset of strs containing at most m zeros and n ones.
Idea: Count each string's zeros and ones and update a 0/1 knapsack table in descending capacity order.
Technique and why it applies: dp[i][j] stores the best subset count for budgets i zeros and j ones. Reversing both loops ensures each string contributes at most once per DP iteration.
Invariant: Every state is the maximum count achievable using the strings processed up to the current one.
Edge cases: The table is dimensioned by zero budget m and one budget n. The code's indentation includes a tab before the inner loop; mixed tabs and spaces can cause Python indentation errors depending on the exact file bytes.
Complexity: Each string updates O(mn) states, giving O(Wmn) time and O(mn) DP space, matching the space label.

Task and constraints: Find the smallest heater radius that warms every house, given house and heater positions on a line.
Idea: Sort both position lists, then use binary search to find the nearest heater at or to the right of each house and compare it with the previous heater.
Technique and why it applies: The distance to the nearest heater is the minimum of the distances to adjacent heaters in sorted order. The largest of these nearest distances is the required radius.
Invariant: max_radius is the greatest nearest-heater distance seen among processed houses.
Edge cases: The snippet references inf and bisect_left without importing them, so it fails unless those names are defined externally. It assumes at least one heater; otherwise heaters[-1] fails for houses to the right.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(H log H + R log R), and each house query is O(log R), for O(H log H + R log R) time and O(1) explicit extra space aside from sorting.

Task and constraints: Determine the minimum uniform radius covering all houses using the available heater locations.
Idea: Sort heater positions and binary-search each house's insertion point to compare nearest left and right heaters.
Technique and why it applies: bisect_left finds the first heater not left of the house. The code measures distance to that heater when present and to the preceding heater when present, then takes the maximum nearest distance across houses.
Invariant: min_radius stores the greatest minimum distance from any processed house to a heater.
Edge cases: The method assumes heaters is nonempty; otherwise a house has no possible nearest heater. Houses are not sorted because binary search is performed on the heater list only.
Complexity: Sorting heaters is O(R log R) and each of H houses uses O(log R) search, so O(R log R + H log R) time and O(1) explicit auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the bitwise complement of a positive integer using only its significant binary digits.
Idea: Find the smallest power of two greater than num, then subtract num and one from that power.
Technique and why it applies: If num uses i bits, 2^i-1 is a mask of i ones. Subtracting num from that mask flips each significant bit, equivalent to complementing the binary representation without leading zeros.
Invariant: i is the bit width of num after the loop terminates.
Edge cases: The code assumes num is positive; for zero, the loop leaves i=0 and returns zero, though problem constraints generally exclude zero. Very large values use arbitrary-precision integers.
Complexity: The loop takes O(log num) iterations and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the complement of num within its significant binary width.
Idea: Find the smallest power of two strictly greater than num, form an all-ones mask below it, and XOR that mask with num.
Technique and why it applies: Repeated doubling computes the width boundary i; i-1 contains ones in exactly the positions needed. XOR flips all significant bits while leaving no extra leading bits.
Invariant: i is the first power of two greater than num.
Edge cases: For num=5, i becomes 8 and mask 7 flips the three low bits. For num=0, the code returns 0, though the standard problem usually specifies a positive integer.
Complexity: The shift loop is O(log num) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Flip all bits in the binary representation of num, considering only its significant digits.
Idea: Format the integer as binary text, swap each 0 with 1 and each 1 with 0, then parse the resulting bit string.
Technique and why it applies: The format string omits leading zeros, so the generated complement has exactly the same width as the original binary representation.
Invariant: complement_bits contains the bitwise inverse of every character in bits.
Edge cases: The code assumes num is nonnegative. For num=0, format yields '0b0' only if a prefix format were used; here '{0:b}' yields '0', so it returns 1 as the complement of the one-bit representation.
Complexity: Formatting, mapping, joining, and parsing take O(log num) time and O(log num) extra space.
